title: Africa’s green industrialization blind spot: politics
body:
Africa’s green industrialization debate is often technical: megawatts installed, minerals extracted, grids expanded, factories built. But green industrialization don’t entirely fail because of spreadsheets. They often fail because of politics.

Green industrialization is not a neutral upgrade of technologies. It reshapes power, reallocates rents, and disrupts livelihoods.

This raises uncomfortable questions that policy documents often sidestep: Who gains? Who loses? Who resists?

When these questions are ignored, the outcomes are predictable:

- Pushback from incumbents whose rents are threatened
- Social resistance to infrastructure that excludes or displaces communities
- Policy reversals when costs become politically visible and benefits remain abstract

This is not a design flaw. It is a political economy reality.

Successful green industrialization strategies anticipate these questions rather than deny it. Hence they:

- Build credible transition pathways for affected workers and firms
- Share benefits through local content, community ownership, and jobs
- Sequence reforms to maintain political coalitions, not just technical efficiency

Green industrialization is not just about cleaner energy and low carbon technologies; it is about restructuring economies and redistributing opportunities.

If Africa wants its green industrialization to endure, it must be politically sustainable, not only environmentally sound.

The hardest part of green industrialization is not building turbines or grids. It is building consensus, compensation, and credibility.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Solomon Owusu Woubet Kassa, PhD Emmanuel Buadi Mensah Victor Osei Kwadwo, Ph.D. Hubert Nii-Aponsah, PhD Davina Osei
